pages.text: The Ansah family lived in a modest three-bedroom house with a small gate and a mango tree. Mrs Ansah was a nurse, Mr Ansah was a senior teacher, and their children went to a private school. To the neighbours, they looked comfortable. Theophilus believed it too, until the last week of the month, when everything went quiet and nobody asked for ice cream.

pages.text: At month-end, Theophilus noticed things. His mother walked to work instead of taking a taxi. His father counted coins at the kitchen table. The data bundle ran out. A slip in his school bag reminded him that the second instalment of fees was due. “Do not worry,” his mother said, but her smile did not reach her eyes.

pages.alt: A boy watches his father count coins at a kitchen table with a fee slip beside him.

pages.text: At school, Theophilus hid the slip. His friends talked about holidays abroad and new phones, and he laughed along, afraid to be different. He told Vida, “Do not tell anyone we are short.” “But why?” she asked. “Because they will think we are poor,” he whispered. Vida frowned. “Is being short of money the same as being poor?” she asked. Theophilus had no answer.

pages.alt: A boy whispers to his younger sister at school gates while other students chat nearby.

pages.text: That weekend, Theophilus heard his parents talking softly in the kitchen. His father said, “We must either delay the fees or borrow, and I do not like borrowing.” His mother said, “Then we write to the school and explain honestly.” Theophilus stepped in. “Maybe I can help,” he said. His parents were surprised. “You are old enough to know,” said his father gently.

pages.text: Mr Ansah opened his accounts book. “Income, expenses, savings,” he said. “We earn this much. Fees, rent, food, transport, data, medicine. We are not poor, but there is little left. Every cedi must have a job.” He showed Theophilus where they had trimmed spending: fewer takeaways, no new clothes. “We do this together,” he said. “And we talk about money without shame.”

pages.text: Together they wrote a formal letter to the head teacher. At the top right, Mr Ansah put his address, House 7, Mango Close, Kumasi, and below it the date, 28th February, 2027. On the left: The Head Teacher, Ridgeview Preparatory School, Box 31, Kumasi. “Dear Madam,” the letter began, and the heading read: REQUEST TO PAY THE SECOND INSTALMENT OF SCHOOL FEES IN TWO PARTS. The body read: “I am writing to request that I be allowed to pay the second instalment of Theophilus’s fees in two parts, one on 5th March and the other on 20th March. Firstly, my family’s expenses this month have been higher than usual. Secondly, I have paid every previous instalment on time. I shall be grateful for your kind consideration.” He closed with “Yours faithfully,” signed, and wrote his full name, Gabriel Ansah.

The body read: “I am writing to request that I be allowed to pay the second instalment of Theophilus’s fees in two parts, one on 5th March and the other on 20th March.
Firstly, my family’s expenses this month have been higher than usual.
Secondly, I have paid every previous instalment on time.
I shall be grateful for your kind consideration.” He closed with “Yours faithfully,” signed, and wrote his full name, Gabriel Ansah.
pages.alt: A father and son write a formal letter at a table, with an address and date at the top.

pages.text: The head teacher replied within two days. She agreed, and she also told the family about a school hardship fund for any child in need. “You did the right thing by asking,” she said. “Asking early is a sign of responsibility.” Theophilus felt the knot in his stomach loosen. At school, he told his closest friend the truth. “My family does not have as much as you think,” he said. His friend only said, “Mine neither.”

The body is polite, clear and persuasive, with two reasons, and uses no contractions or slang. Check the eight features before you hand in a formal letter. The end.
